1: # VEPU510 H.264 encoder
2: 
3: The driver encodes one picture at a time and predicts each picture from the
4: reconstruction of the picture before it.  What that is worth, and how long a
5: group of pictures it is worth doing it over, was measured rather than assumed;
6: this file records the measurement.
7: 
8: ## Group length
9: 
10: A group is one IDR followed by pictures that predict from it and from each
11: other, so its length is what decides how much of a stream is the expensive
12: kind.  Two questions get two answers here: the driver's default is two
13: pictures (`RK3576_VEPU_DEFAULT_GOP`) and the streaming application asks for
14: fifteen (`CAMENC_DEFAULT_GOP`).  The driver does not know how its stream is
15: consumed, so it takes the shortest group that predicts at all; the
16: application does know, so it takes the group that is worth having and pays for
17: it knowingly.
18: 
19: ### Measured after the fault was fixed
20: 
21: This is the number to use.  1296x960 at quantiser 26, thirty frames a second,
22: on a source the encoder is asked to draw itself -- one constant background
23: with a small square moving slowly round it -- over 597 pictures.  Payload
24: bytes, so the container is not counted:
25: 
26: | pictures per group | IDR | P | payload | rate |
27: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
28: | 2 | 299 at 31350 B | 298 at 253 B | 9449442 B | 3799 kbit/s |
29: | 4 | 150 at 31368 B | 447 at 248 B | 4816531 B | **1937 kbit/s** |
30: 
31: Doubling the group halves the rate -- four is 51.0% of two -- and where the
32: bytes are says why.  Half the groups at two open with an IDR; a quarter of
33: them at four do.  Nothing else stands out, because a P is under one per cent
34: of an IDR and no P differs much from its neighbours:
35: 
36: | position in the group | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
37: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
38: | mean bytes | 31368 | 256 | 238 | 250 |
39: 
40: The quality is not what is being spent.  Decoding both streams and comparing
41: every picture with the source gives an RMSE of 0.78, and it is 0.78 for the
42: IDR and for each of the three P positions of a four-picture group: nothing
43: accumulates through the group.
44: 
45: Two numbers are enough to say what a longer group would do, because the rate
46: is `fps * 8 * (IDR/G + P)`: 3824 and 1942 kbit/s for two and four against the
47: 3799 and 1937 measured, and 561 for fifteen.  What that also says is where
48: the model stops being the answer.  The only term that falls with the group is
49: the IDR's, and it falls as 1/G, so the rate keeps improving -- but the price
50: of a long group is not in the rate.  A decoder that joined late, or that
51: missed a fragment, has to wait for the next picture a stream may start on,
52: which is one group away, and a fragment missed is not one picture lost but
53: everything up to that next start.
54: 
55: Fifteen is where those meet for a stream watched live: half a second at
56: thirty frames a second, which is a hiccup and not a wait, and far enough along
57: the curve that the rate is already a thirteenth of all-intra's.  Doubling it
58: again would take another 251 kbit/s off and add another half second to every
59: client's wait -- which is the trade, stated in the numbers it is made in.
60: 
61: ### Measured before it was fixed, which is what the fault looked like
62: 
63: The same measurement was taken on a 640x480 capture of a static scene -- a
64: ceiling light, no motion in frame, 60 frames, quantiser 26, no rate control --
65: while the encoder carried the fault described below.  It said a long group was
66: not worth having:
67: 
68: | pictures per group | IDR | P | payload | rate | against all-intra |
69: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
70: | 1 (all intra) | 60 | 0 | 186680 B | 1454 kbit/s | -- |
71: | 2 | 30 | 30 | 95862 B | 747 kbit/s | **-48.7%** |
72: | 4 | 15 | 45 | 90487 B | 705 kbit/s | -51.5% |
73: 
74: The all-intra row is not a capture.  It is the IDR mean of the other two
75: multiplied by 60, which is sound because the IDR mean is the same at both
76: group lengths to within 0.03% (3111 B against 3110 B) -- the cost of an IDR
77: does not depend on what surrounds it.
78: 
79: **Two was where the saving was.**  Going from one picture per group to two
80: took 48.7% off the rate, and it all came from the P pictures: a P was 84 bytes
81: where an IDR was 3111, which is 2.7%.
82: 
83: **Four was not.**  Doubling the group again halved the number of IDRs and
84: bought 5.6%.  The per-frame sizes said why:
85: 
86: ```
87: I 3010   p 100   p 3384   p  14
88: I 3006   p  12   p 3380   p  12
89: I 3014   p   9   p 3370   p  16
90: ```
91: 
92: One P in every group cost as much as the IDR that opened it -- 3380 bytes
93: against 3010 -- and those frames were worth 42415 of the 47830 bytes that
94: doubling the group saved.  Had they been as cheap as the P pictures at two per
95: group, four per group would have come out at 374 kbit/s; instead it came out
96: at 705.
97: 
98: Nothing was wrong with the streams, which is what made this look like a
99: property of the content: decoding both captures and comparing them frame for
100: frame gave an RMSE of about 1.1 out of 255 for every frame after the first
101: two, and within a group the reconstruction never got more than 1.2 RMSE away
102: from the IDR that opened it.
103: 
104: **The expensive P was the fault.**  It is explained now.  The register layer
105: programmed the anti-smear stage from the previous picture's state, which is
106: what the newer vendor code does and what the 1.0.6 library this driver was
107: measured against does not; with that state in force, a picture predicted from
108: a reference with its own local mean taken out of it.  The residual that leaves
109: is wrong, so the rate-distortion decision finds prediction not worth taking
110: and codes those pictures almost as intra -- which is exactly a P that costs
111: what an IDR costs, on content whose P pictures are otherwise nearly free.
112: Writing the 1.0.6 constants instead made both symptoms go: the pictures, which
113: had been drifting by the reference's own mean, and the rate.  The change is in
114: the driver's history.  A note on `rk3576_vepu_selftest_sequence()`, in
115: `rk3576_vepu.c`, describes a synthetic source on which the same thing used to
116: happen far more severely; that source is pathological -- a hard vertical edge
117: walking across the frame -- and is close to the worst input a predictive
118: encoder can be given.  It is kept as a canary, not as evidence about a scene.
119: 
120: Both tables are kept because they are the two halves of one lesson: a fault in
121: the prediction of P pictures shows up as a rate as much as as a picture, and
122: the rate finding was read as a fact about the content for as long as the
123: picture finding was read as a separate bug.
124: 
125: ## Upstream
126: 
127: Rockchip's own answer, in `rockchip-linux/mpp` issue #211 ("1080@30fps in
128: 2 Mbps encoding has ghosting"), was that the encoder has a strong preference
129: for coding skip pictures and that the resulting artefacts are not something MPP
130: is responsible for -- the reporter was told to raise it on their redmine
131: instead, with their FAE.  The same "a skip picture cannot be a reference"
132: mechanism is visible in MPP's source: it carries a `force_pskip_is_ref` option
133: in both its H.264 and its H.265 encoder, and its H.265 decoder picture buffer
134: has a comment about holding a reference buffer as a skip picture's
135: reconstruction buffer.  That option is off by default.  Issue #961, on this
136: same silicon with a long group, is open and unresolved.
137: 
138: None of this is a workaround, and none of it is what this driver had: the
139: fault above was in the state the driver programmed, not in the silicon's
140: handling of skip pictures.  It is kept here because a long group is what makes
141: the question worth asking -- issue #961 is a report of horizontal bars from
142: this encoder, on this silicon, with a long group, and it is unresolved.
143: 
144: ## The self-test
145: 
146: `rk3576_vepu_selftest()` runs at boot when `CONFIG_RK3576_VEPU_SELFTEST` is
147: set, and is the reason several of the above claims are checkable rather than
148: asserted.  It has two halves, and it runs the sequence test first because what
149: that test observes is the state before any picture has been encoded -- no
150: reference to predict from.
151: 
152:   * The **sequence test** encodes a moving source as an IDR followed by P
153:     pictures and checks that a P comes out cheaper than its own reference.
154:     Failing that check means prediction has stopped working, which is the
155:     failure that is otherwise silent: the stream still decodes, it is just at
156:     the wrong rate.
157:   * The **picture test** encodes static, gradient and noise sources and checks
158:     that the sizes come out in the order the sources' complexity implies, and
159:     that a NAL ends where the encoder said it did.
160: 
161: `CONFIG_RK3576_VEPU_SEQ_DUMP` adds a hex dump of the coded stream, which is
162: not on by default because it is for reading with a decoder rather than from a
163: terminal.
164: 
165: ## What it prints at boot
166: 
167: Five lines, and nothing else:
168: 
169: ```
170: VEPU0: aclk=... hclk=... core=... (targets ... and ...)
171: VEPU0: VEPU510 rev ..., ip_id 0x..., h264=... hevc=... bframe=... fbc=..., res=..., osd=..., filter=...
172: VEPU0 sequence test: N frames, N bytes: IDR N B mean, P N B mean (N% of an IDR)
173: VEPU0 self-test: N frames, N bytes of bitstream, solid L/s, gradient L/s, noise L/s
174: VEPU0 codec self-test: N frames through the device node, N bytes of bitstream
175: ```
176: 
177: They report the two facts worth having at every boot -- which IP answered,
178: and whether the encode path works -- once for each layer that can break
179: independently: the hardware, the encode path, and the device node an
180: application actually talks to.  The clock rates are there because a core
181: clock left on its reset source makes the encoder work at a fraction of its
182: speed and say nothing about it.
183: 
184: The sequence test's line is the one to read if a stream is larger than it
185: should be: it reports the mean P picture against the mean IDR, and a P that
186: is not a small fraction of an IDR means prediction has stopped being used,
187: which is a failure that decodes correctly and only shows as size.
188: 
189: Everything else the driver knows -- which clock source each branch settled
190: on, what the dividers hold, the size of the reconstruction sets, a
191: frame-by-frame account of both self-tests -- goes through `vinfo()`, which
192: NuttX enables with `CONFIG_DEBUG_VIDEO_INFO` (its video subsystem debug
193: switch, off by default).  The detail is kept rather than deleted, so that it
194: can be asked for; it just is not printed twenty-odd lines at a time in front
195: of whatever does deserve attention.
196: 
197: Errors are not affected: `_err` is reported whatever the debug options say,
198: and `rk3576_vepu_dump()` prints the registers when an encode fails.
199:

=== README.md ===
# VEPU510 H.264 encoder

The driver encodes one picture at a time and predicts each picture from the
reconstruction of the picture before it.  What that is worth, and how long a
group of pictures it is worth doing it over, was measured rather than assumed;
this file records the measurement.

## Group length

A group is one IDR followed by pictures that predict from it and from each
other, so its length is what decides how much of a stream is the expensive
kind.  Two questions get two answers here: the driver's default is two
pictures (`RK3576_VEPU_DEFAULT_GOP`) and the streaming application asks for
fifteen (`CAMENC_DEFAULT_GOP`).  The driver does not know how its stream is
consumed, so it takes the shortest group that predicts at all; the
application does know, so it takes the group that is worth having and pays for
it knowingly.

### Measured after the fault was fixed

This is the number to use.  1296x960 at quantiser 26, thirty frames a second,
on a source the encoder is asked to draw itself -- one constant background
with a small square moving slowly round it -- over 597 pictures.  Payload
bytes, so the container is not counted:

output:
# Nyabula · 星喵

### 基于 openvela 的 RK3576 桌面 AI 陪伴猫

**2026 首届 openvela AI 硬件开发者大赛 · 队伍 062 · Pharos Tech**

参赛方向：**新硬件适配 + AI 硬件产品创新**

Nyabula 是一只用双圆屏表达情绪、能听懂指令并执行设备动作的桌面陪伴猫。我们从 KICKPI-K7 的第一行串口输出开始，把 openvela 移植到 RK3576，逐步完成存储、原生 WiFi/蓝牙、音频、USB、双屏、启动恢复和产品运行时，最终打通 **唤醒 → 语音识别 → Agent → 工具执行或回答 → 语音合成 → 扬声器播报** 的完整交互回合。

设备可以使用 RK3576 NPU 上的本地 MiniCPM5-1B，也已接通小米 MiMo 在线 Agent。**openvela 负责产品状态、权限、工具执行、记忆、联网、存储、双眼和音频；Linux 通过 AMP 提供模型与摄像头计算服务。** 我们同时把开发过程沉淀为 24 份工程 Skill、构建与调试工具、可追溯的 PR 和 AI Coding 日志，希望交付一只可演示的猫，也交付一套其他团队能够继续使用的移植方法。

> **版本口径：2026-09-20，UTC+8。** 本文覆盖团队已完成的主线、产品分支和独立实验成果，并分别标明证据范围。完整语音功能由当日现场验收确认；产品集成在 [PR #93][p93]，尚未合入。24 份工程 Skill、双方 AI 日志与示例清理已分别经 [#95][p95]、[#96][p96]、[#98][p98]、[#97][p97] 合入。本文不是某一个最终镜像的全功能长稳认证。

**快速入口：** [作品亮点](#作品亮点) · [产品体验](#产品体验) · [架构](#系统架构) · [硬件与BSP](#硬件平台与-bsp) · [语音与Agent](#完整语音与双后端-agent) · [实测数据](#实测数据与验证范围) · [构建运行](#获取构建与运行) · [24份Skill](#24-份可复用工程-skill) · [交付状态](#交付状态与下一步)

## 作品亮点

| 亮点 | 我们完成了什么 | 为什么有价值 |
|---|---|---|
| 新 ARM64 平台适配 | 以 RK3399 移植为参考，完成 RK3576 的启动、GICv2、MMU、时钟、SMP/AMP 与外设适配 | 将高性能 Rockchip 平台接入 openvela，留下芯片层、板级层与设备驱动的清晰边界 |
| 原生无线 | SV6621/SWT6621S FullMAC WiFi 和 SDIO 蓝牙 transport；STA、SoftAP、WPA3 等独立板测 | openvela 自己持有无线与网络能力，计算域无需代管 WiFi |
| 完整语音产品链 | 本地唤醒、ASR、Agent、工具执行、TTS 和播报贯通；支持端侧与在线模型后端 | 从“模型能运行”推进到“设备能回应、能做事” |
| 异构协作 | 4×A53 openvela + 4×A72 Linux 拓扑、RPMsg、共享内存、模型按需传递 | 保留 openvela 的产品控制权，同时利用 RK3576 NPU 与 Linux 模型生态 |
| 可维护的设备 | N-Boot、NuttX/AMP 双域 A/B、摘要校验、Fastboot、运行态 nbootctl、面板 OTA | 从拔卡烧写演进为可持续开发、部署与恢复的设备 |
| 双眼与产品运行时 | 双 GC9B72 圆屏、Eye Engine、权限 Broker、JS/Wasm 插件、原生产品服务和自托管面板 | 把表情、状态、工具和交互统一到一个设备运行时 |
| AI 开发方法可复用 | 24 份工程 Skill；源码、反例、验证脚本、来源与边界一起交付 | 将一次比赛中的探索变成下一块板、下一个驱动可复用的工程知识 |

## 产品体验

### 已贯通的交互主线

1. **连接设备。** 通过设备 SoftAP 配网、二维码入口和浏览器控制台完成联网与设置。控制台由设备自身托管，HTTP 与 WebSocket 共享服务端口。
2. **看见反馈。** 双眼显示表情、凝视、眨眼、字幕和状态场景，语音回合中的聆听、处理与播报有对应视觉状态。
3. **自然说话。** 唤醒后采集语音、识别文本，交给同一个 Nyabot/官方 `ai_agent` 工具执行链；回复合成为声音并播放。赛事唤醒词遵循“你好，openvela / Hello, openvela”的要求。
4. **执行真实动作。** 已测的端侧指令包括读取时间、显示开心表情、创建五分钟计时器、设置或相对调整音量、写入长期记忆、建立闹钟与待办。设备状态实际变化，并返回 `sideEffectApplied:true`。
5. **选择模型后端。** 本地 MiniCPM5-1B 负责端侧回答与受约束的设备意图处理；在线 MiMo 已完成 HTTPS 调用和多工具成功回合。两类后端使用产品侧的权限和工具机制。
6. **持续维护。** 面板可管理设置、模型与升级；AMP 运行期间已经实测上传新固件、写非运行 AMP 槽、重启与确认。

以上语音主链、端侧工具动作、在线 Agent、面板和 OTA 各有当日功能验证；没有将其扩张成所有后端、异常、打断和并发组合均已完成测试。

### 使用场景与产品方向

Nyabula 面向桌面工作、学习与日常陪伴：用眼睛提供轻量反馈，用语音完成计时、提醒和设备控制，用可扩展工具连接其他服务。端侧模型为本地交互提供基础，在线模型扩展复杂语言处理能力。插件、MCP 和工程 Skill 则让设备具备继续扩展的空间。

当前定位是具有完整交互主线的工程原型。面向开发者的 openvela/Rockchip 参考平台与可扩展陪伴终端，是两条可继续探索的产品方向；成本、续航、量产结构和商业定价尚未完成验证。

## 系统架构

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  User[用户：语音 / 浏览器] --> V
  subgraph V[openvela / NuttX：产品控制域]
    Voice[麦克风采集 / 预录 / 语音回合 / 播放]
    Core[Nyabula Core：状态 / 权限 / 插件 / 记忆]
    Agent[Nyabot + 官方 ai_agent]
    Devices[双眼 / WiFi / 音频 / eMMC / USB / 时钟]
    Panel[设备自托管 Web / NyaLink / MCP]
    Voice <--> Agent
    Agent <--> Core
    Core <--> Devices
    Panel <--> Core
  end
  subgraph L[Linux：AMP 计算域]
    Daemon[nyampd 计算服务]
    AI[KWS / ASR / G2P与TTS / RKLLM / NPU]
    Camera[CSI 摄像头 / 视觉实验]
    Daemon <--> AI
    Daemon <--> Camera
  end
  Core <-->|RPMsg 控制 + 共享内存数据| Daemon
  Voice <-->|采集与PCM窗口| Daemon
  Agent <-->|HTTPS| MiMo[小米 MiMo 在线模型]
  Boot[N-Boot：启动 / A-B槽 / 恢复] --> V
  Boot --> L
```

### 为什么把产品控制放在 openvela

设备的状态、文件、权限与执行结果由 openvela 管理。模型提出回答或动作请求，实际调用仍经过产品工具和审批逻辑；Linux 提供计算结果，不直接接管产品状态数据库。在线模型接通后，同样沿用这一机制。
